extracted.intended_audience: newspaper reporters and journalism students who cover local theater, music, books, and obituaries
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for reporting and critiquing local theatrical productions, musical events, book reviews, and obituaries for community newspapers, emphasizing story structure, sourcing, tone, and ethical/technical procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be specific in praise and criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid vague laudatory or pejorative labels (e.g., 'superb', 'hopeless'). Instead, make judgments specific and tell how someone was superb or why something failed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example rewrite: instead of 'Ida Elwell was superb,' write 'Her enthusiasm in the spelling-bee scene and her delight at winning third prize were the liveliest bits in the show.' Specifics give readers who saw the show confirmation and those who haven't something to watch for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include names of behind-the-scenes workers
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of cameramen, wardrobe custodians, carpenters, stagehands, electricians, and other backstage crew belong in the story and are especially valuable in home-grown shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the craftsmen's work materially affects the production (e.g., set and painting making the audience 'smell the Hudson River'), include their names; obtain missing names from programs or by extra effort—it's worth it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theater-story block structure (Blocks 1–8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize a theater story into defined blocks: Block 1 — the five Ws; Block 2 — names of chief characters and roles (no comment unless specific); Block 3 — secondary characters and roles (no comment unless specific); Block 4 — explicit description of the show tied to a central theme or impression; Block 5 — names of backstage crews; Block 6 — chorus or battle-scene members; Block 7 — musicians; Block 8 — director, coach, publicity chairman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a usually minor group has unexpected interest, lift its block higher. Use this structure to ensure completeness (sample story provided). Keep judgments explicit rather than vague.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague/general commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make general, unsupported judgments about a performance; every judgment should be explicit and tied to specifics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers care about the play more than stylistic flourishes from the reporter. Provide concrete examples of what made a moment effective or ineffective rather than glossing with generic praise or condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve harsh criticism; allocate unfavorable criticism carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not pan a performance lightly, because that insults audience taste; when criticism is necessary allocate blame carefully (e.g., sometimes the playwright—not the actor—deserves the fault).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially in local/home-grown productions be cautious with harsh language; for professionals use stricter standards but still be fair and precise in attributing faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different standards for professional vs. home-grown shows
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional stage or film should be judged by more rigid criteria than community or school productions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of differing expectations; also avoid conflicts of interest (e.g., accepting passes/admissions that might influence willingness to criticize). Some offices pay reporters' way to avoid bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use publicity as source material—rewrite, don't paste
rubrics_metrics.description: Movie and publicity copy (Hollywood puffery) should be used only as source material and must be rewritten—dropping excessive laudatory adjectives—so it becomes human-interest or feature matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convert puffery into local or human-interest angles; do not paste studio publicity verbatim into your column. Example: drop 'nine-and-ninety laudatory adjectives' and recast as useful local material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring local material into columns
rubrics_metrics.description: Enrich columns with local angles: theater managers, projection staff, ushers, stagehands, guild committees, and patrons provide story material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local anecdotes or managerial insights (e.g., a manager explaining local tastes) make columns legitimate features rather than free advertising; when done poorly they can become inadvertent promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of critic's power and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic may influence audience attendance and the fortunes of local theater companies; vicious or careless reviews can kill a company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise restraint and fairness; excessive viciousness may destroy local arts resources and shrink the newspaper's theater coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop and use local music sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Build a sizable list of sources for music stories, including: (1) music teachers (recitals), (2) music students (interesting individuals), (3) school and lodge orchestras/bands, (4) church music/choir directors, (5) concerts and recitals, (6) contests/competitions, (7) local music clubs and organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat community music as a legitimate beat; many story opportunities come from these groups if the reporter looks for local angles and background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish reporting from technical criticism in music coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting: description of what happened in nontechnical language; Criticism: evaluation of technical accomplishment and interpretation, which may be understood only by musically trained readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For most community papers favor reporting (accessible descriptions) but include some technical commentary for informed readers when appropriate. Be explicit in judgments and explain technical faults kindly, avoiding sarcasm—particularly with youngsters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-track music-story structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested structure: Block 1 — the five Ws; Block 2 — nontechnical paragraph describing the event in ordinary language; Block 3 — technical section characterizing the performance in musicians' language; Block 4 — program analysis in ordinary language (e.g., classical vs popular balance); Block 5 — program analysis in technical language for musician readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blocks 2–5 can be reordered depending on whether the larger general audience or the smaller musically trained audience should be favored. Use explicit, kind explanations of technical faults when presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit and kind with critiques of youngsters
rubrics_metrics.description: When commenting on performances by children or students avoid sarcasm and belittlement; either overlook small lapses or praise recovery and improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Young performers can be emotionally harmed by harsh reviews; point out strengths or constructive specifics rather than ridicule stage fright or mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book-review beat: adapt to local constraints and audience
rubrics_metrics.description: If review copies are scarce, run isolated reviews rather than attempting comprehensive coverage. Write for the 'ordinary reader' rather than scholarly specialists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge books for their ability to interest everyday readers (pleasure reading) rather than for scholarly merit; if a book requires specialized knowledge, farm it out to a qualified consultant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book-review reading and writing practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignore jacket blurbs as unreliable; read some books closely and others by skimming typical passages; write in easy, natural English and avoid needlessly erudite vocabulary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not 'write down' to readers but keep sentences lucid and accessible. Provide an overall quality label (e.g., 'good (fair) (poor) reading') and back it with clear reasons rather than scholarly comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use consultants for specialized books
rubrics_metrics.description: When a book calls for expertise beyond the reviewer's knowledge, recruit qualified local consultants to write the review or advise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build a corps of consultants (e.g., a local who lived in a region discussed in the book) to ensure accurate evaluation of specialized subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obituaries: extreme care with accuracy and taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Obituaries are read, clipped, and saved; mistakes (wrong affiliations, wrong lodges, wrong photos) cause lasting offense and damage to the paper's reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be scrupulous about facts and tasteful phrasing; families judge the paper by how careful it was during their sorrow. High-quality obit work is a valued skill in a reporter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle advance obituaries with strict controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Advance obits prepared in case of eminent deaths must be clearly labeled 'Hold for Release' (or similar), proofed to show the hold line, and the proof retained as evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure composing room and make-up personnel preserve the hold notice; obtain and save the proof showing the warning to protect against accidental publication and to assign responsibility if a premature print occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obit photographs: preserve, verify, and return promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: When collecting family photos for obits, mark and protect them, retrieve proofs from engravers, inspect make-up to avoid transposition, and return photos quickly—ideally personally if the office system is unreliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label photos ('Obit — handle carefully'), check proof cuts and proofs to ensure correct identification, and inspect early press runs to catch transpositions. Prompt, careful return avoids long-term damage to the paper's reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build obituary coverage through undertaker cooperation and verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Work to ensure undertakers report deaths promptly; supply them with biographical blanks to fill in; learn undertakers' voices to detect bogus calls; never run an unverified death notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat undertakers as primary, dependable sources and verify any suspicious calls by follow-up (e.g., telephone to confirm service times). Do not allow prank or false announcements into print.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical newsroom ethics to avoid conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Be wary of relationships that may influence coverage (e.g., free passes, advertising pressure from movie houses); where possible pay your own way to preserve independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some offices give reporters money for tickets; otherwise the reporter should pay to avoid feelings of obligation. Apply stricter judgment to paid or promotional events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize readers' needs over stylistic display
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'scintillating writing' or overly ornate vocabulary at the expense of conveying useful information about the event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers are more interested in what happened in the play, concert, or book than in the reporter's linguistic flourishes; clarity, explicitness, and usefulness are paramount.
